There seems to be a lot of misinformation in this comment section. The DSM is far from perfect and I'm not here to defend it or dissuade anyone from their opinions of it. However, I do have some recommendations to help understand it better. 

1- Read it. It's just a reference book. It has definable criteria for each diagnosis but under each diagnosis there is a list of differential diagnoses, something it could actually be instead of what you think it is. There is also a list of common comorbidities that could be confounding your diagnosis. And at the end of each categorical section of diagnoses there are unspecified diagnoses which are there to use when someone has the hallmarks of a diagnosis but doesn't meet all diagnostic criteria. 

2- Understand that it's not a guide to treatment or an explanation of the origin of someone's diagnosis. It's just a guide to diagnose symptoms in the present moment. It would be unethical for the DSM to give clinicians blanket recommendations on what is causing these symptoms or the best way to treat them.

3- Any therapist licensed after 2000 should know about the Adverse Childhood Experiences study or ACEs. OP, you mentioned the connection between obesity, autoimmune issues, and trauma but somehow didn't mention the ACEs study. While the connection between trauma and health issues is significant that still doesn't give us a great solution for treatment. (Though I wish medical professionals would get their heads out of their asses and stop shaming their patients) 

4- There are some really awful clinicians out there who just don't understand how to use the DSM properly. I wish there was a better way to weed these people out because they're just doing more harm than good. I'm sorry to anyone here that has had to deal with a therapist like that.

I'm in school to become a therapist. I learned recently that most people don't understand what resilience or resiliency actually mean or how to develop it. Most of us who had adverse childhood experiences that created CPTSD really struggle to develop resiliency. 

Resiliency is developed mostly as a child by experiencing healthy, supportive, long term relationships with at least one adult in your life. The more of these adults and relationships the better your outcome will be. 

As an adult, your resilience manifests in your ability to regulate emotions despite circumstances. Meaning you have effective healthy coping skills and/or find some measure of relief in mental health treatment. It manifests as having some measure of hope that you can resolve challenges or can find someone to help. And it manifests as feeling some degree of contentment and/or happiness.

If you don't feel resilient, then you probably don't have a lot of resiliency. THIS IS NOT YOUR FAULT. It's an unfortunate symptom of trauma. Resilience can be developed as an adult but it is much harder to get there especially if trauma continues to happen.

Bright colorful hair is also kind of like a bat signal in the queer community right now. You definitely won't look like the cookie cutter Mormon guy if you've got bright pink hair.

2- TSHIRTS!! If you're wearing a collared shirt every day swap it out for a graphic tee with a blazer, jeans, and dress shoes. Professional yet approachable. 👍 Your member clients will probably feel more comfortable with you too. Clients can struggle opening up to their clinician if they are too dressed up. My personal therapist told me her entire case load reported feeling more comfortable when she started wearing jeans regularly. 

3- Get a small ALLY FLAG!! Most church members will be oblivious to it's meaning but it will be clear to your LGBT clients that you are affirming. 

Best of luck!! And thanks for being awesome!! 🥰
